## Overview

The Six Sided Die represents a discrete uniform distribution. Unlike the Standard Normal, this population is not bell-shaped — it has exactly six equally likely outcomes (1 through 6). However it is symmetric, which means we expect the CLT to kick in relatively quickly compared to skewed distributions.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup

set.seed(1278)
B <- 10000
library(moments)
```

## 1. What Does the Population Look Like?

```{r}
#| label: population-plot

barplot(rep(1/6, 6), names.arg = 1:6,
        col = "steelblue", border = "white",
        main = "Six Sided Die Population",
        xlab = "Outcome", ylab = "Probability")
```

The Six Sided Die has six equally likely outcomes. It is discrete and uniform — every value between 1 and 6 has exactly a 1/6 chance of occurring.

**Theoretical mean:** (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5\
**Theoretical standard deviation:** sqrt(35/12) ≈ 1.708

## 2. My Prediction

Since this distribution is symmetric (just not normal), I expect the CLT to work fairly quickly — probably around n = 10 to 20. The symmetry means there is no skew to overcome, so the sampling distribution should approach normality faster than skewed distributions like the Exponential.

## 3. Monte Carlo Simulation

```{r}
#| label: simulation

n_values <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100)

results <- data.frame(
  n              = n_values,
  simulated_mean = NA,
  simulated_sd   = NA,
  theoretical_se = NA,
  skewness       = NA,
  kurtosis       = NA
)

for (i in seq_along(n_values)) {
  n <- n_values[i]
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(sample(1:6, size = n, replace = TRUE)))
  
  results$simulated_mean[i] <- mean(sample_means)
  results$simulated_sd[i]   <- sd(sample_means)
  results$theoretical_se[i] <- sqrt(35/12) / sqrt(n)
  results$skewness[i]       <- skewness(sample_means)
  results$kurtosis[i]       <- kurtosis(sample_means)
}
```

## 4. Results Table

```{r}
#| label: results-table

round(results, 4)
```

## 5. Histograms Across Sample Sizes

```{r}
#| label: histograms
#| fig-height: 10

par(mfrow = c(4, 2))

for (i in seq_along(n_values)) {
  n <- n_values[i]
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(sample(1:6, size = n, replace = TRUE)))
  
  hist(sample_means, breaks = 50, probability = TRUE,
       main = paste("n =", n),
       xlab = "Sample Mean", col = "steelblue", border = "white")
  
  curve(dnorm(x, mean = 3.5, sd = sqrt(35/12) / sqrt(n)),
        add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 6. Q-Q Plots Across Sample Sizes

```{r}
#| label: qqplots
#| fig-height: 10

par(mfrow = c(4, 2))

for (i in seq_along(n_values)) {
  n <- n_values[i]
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(sample(1:6, size = n, replace = TRUE)))
  
  qqnorm(sample_means, main = paste("Q-Q Plot: n =", n),
         col = "steelblue", pch = 20, cex = 0.3)
  qqline(sample_means, col = "red", lwd = 2)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 7. Conclusion

The Six Sided Die sampling distribution converges to normality fairly quickly due to its symmetry. Even though the population is discrete and non-normal, the averaging process smooths things out rapidly.

**My "normal enough" standard:**

- Histogram is visually bell-shaped and symmetric
- Q-Q plot points fall close to the reference line with no systematic curves
- Skewness is between -0.5 and 0.5
- Kurtosis is close to 3

**Answer for Six Sided Die:** $$\boxed{n = 10}$$

By n = 10 the histogram is clearly bell-shaped, the Q-Q plot is approximately linear, and skewness is close to zero. The symmetry of the original distribution means the CLT kicks in much faster than it would for a skewed population.

## 8. What Surprised Me

Even at n = 2, the distribution of sample means already starts losing its uniform shape and showing a triangular bump in the middle. This makes sense — when you average two dice rolls, extreme values (both 1s or both 6s) become less likely than middle values. The CLT is already working at just n = 2, which was faster than I expected for a non-normal population.
